E1015.summary: In Atwood's account, Mammon is the downward-looking spirit that led the depraved abusers of the work astray.
E1015.body: Atwood names Mammon as the spirit that led the depraved abusers of the work: “Mammon led them on; mammon that least erected sprit that fell” [III.4 ¶4]. The phrase pictures it as the least upward-looking spirit.

E1016.summary: A figure that Bacon, writing on Democritus, glosses as laying hold of matter and working on it to the utmost degree.
E1016.body: In Bacon's account of Democritus, quoted in the book, the figure carries its own gloss: “manacles and fetters; i.e., lays hold and works upon matter in the extremist degree” [I.2 ¶23]. The text therefore states the plain meaning: working on matter to the extreme.

E1018.summary: A collection cited as containing works by Philalethes and Grasseus.
E1018.body: Atwood cites Manget's collection as the place where works by Philalethes and Grasseus are found [I.1 ¶73; I.1 n83].

E1019.summary: An author cited from the Astronomicon to support the view that men hold the world within them and are each a small image of God.
E1019.body: Atwood cites Manilius (Astronomicon, lib. 10) in support. He holds that men contain the world within them and are each a small image of God: “Quid mirum noscere mundum” [II.1 ¶29; II.1 n28]. That reading rests on our own translation of the Latin, not one the book gives.

E1020.summary: A practical technique of the work that Ashmole's notes allude to; the book does not describe it here.
E1020.body: Atwood says Ashmole's notes allude to the manual artifice “without much disguise” [I.1 ¶62]. The passage does not describe the technique itself.

E1021.summary: The name for the method of using the key (Kirchringius); for Atwood, the literal handwork needed chiefly in the first work, also called the Linear way.
E1021.body: The book quotes Kirchringius on the key and “the method, which is called Manual Operation, by which to use it” [III.1 ¶37]. Speaking in her own voice, Atwood says that in the first work “Manual operation is chiefly required” [IV.1 ¶2]. She treats it as the one way of Purification, “called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5], and so equates it with the Linear way. Readers took her to mean literal handwork by the operator, but that sense is an inference from context.

forms: manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme's works
E1022.summary: A verse eulogy, found in manuscript in a volume of Boehme's works, praising Boehme for renewing all ancient wisdom; Atwood accepts it with a qualification.
E1022.body: Atwood quotes a manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme's works. It praises Boehme for renewing all ancient wisdom: “In Boehme’s wondrous page we view, Discoverd and revealed anew” [I.1 ¶68]. It names the Eastern Magi, Orpheus, Hermes, Confucius, Zoroaster, Pythagoras, Plato, Socrates and Epictetus [I.1 ¶68–¶70]. Atwood accepts its praise only “theosophically, but not intellectually” [I.1 ¶70].

E1023.summary: A poet whose verse, Atwood says, divulges the artificial method; she says his name means 'one regenerated'. His Zodiacus Vitae is cited on the Ethereal Stone.
E1023.body: Atwood cites Manzoli, called Palingenius, in support. She says his verse divulges the artificial method, quoting “Take this Arcadian slippery lad that’s apt to fly.” [III.1 ¶26]. She also says the name Palingenius means one regenerated [III.1 ¶27]. From the Zodiacus Vitae she cites the art of fashioning the Ethereal Stone: “Invenere artem, qua non ars dignior ulla est, Fingendi Lepidem Aetherium” [IV.3 ¶54; IV.3 n25]. In the readers' account, this art is found only after long trial and cost, is closed to the profane and is granted to few [IV.3 ¶54–¶55].

E1024.summary: Author of the Defensio Idearum Operaticium, cited on the impress and on a plant born, dying and reborn in a glass vessel.
E1024.body: A footnote quotes Marcus's Defensio Idearum Operaticium on the impress and on a plant that is born, dies and is reborn in a glass vessel: “Quid quaesco dicerunt hi tanti philosophi, si plantam quasi momento nasci in vitreo case viderent” [III.3 n27].

E1025.summary: A Hebrew woman advanced in the Hermetic Art, linked with Democritus at Memphis; Atwood often cites her Practica on the matter, the vessel and the order of the work.
E1025.body:
Atwood describes Maria as a Hebrew woman advanced in the Hermetic Art, associated with Democritus at Memphis, whose treatises are extant [I.1 ¶13; I.1 n20]. She cites Maria repeatedly, mostly in support:

- **Matter:** “this science may be found in all bodies”, most easily in matter that plainly holds the four elements [I.3 n48].
- **Order of the work:** Maria illustrates white before red and the rectification of Kibric and Zibeth, which are soul and spirit and the two fumes at the root of the science. Atwood quotes “Take the white, clear, and dignified herb, says Maria, which grows upon the little mountains” [I.3 n67].
- **The vessel:** a divine secret that cannot be done without and is never openly revealed. “Philosophers have spoken sufficiently of all that is necessary concerning the work, with exception of the vessel” [II.1 ¶8; II.1 n1].
- **Shortness of the work:** Maria is cited for the work's shortness as the reason philosophers say little about it [II.1 ¶14].
- **The poison:** once resolved, the deadly poison becomes productive. “when this poison is resolved into a subtle water, it coagulates our Mercury into most pure silver” [III.1 ¶61; III.1 n68].
- **Latin verse:** on fixing the fugitive and binding it in three hours, “Gummis cum binis fugitivum figit in imis,” given without comment [IV.2 ¶31; IV.2 n20].

E1026.summary: Maria's treatise, cited for the vessel of Hermes as the 'measure of thy fire', placed after the Passive Understanding.
E1026.body: Atwood cites the end of the Maria Practica, to support or illustrate the vessel of Hermes as the measure of thy fire, which she places after the Passive Understanding: “Istud est vas Hermetis, quod Stoici occultaverunt” [III.1 ¶40; III.1 n44]. The treatise is cited elsewhere under Maria.

E1027.summary: The union of Mind and Universe, in which solitary Thought unites with the simple Understanding of its ether; ancient mythic marriages prefigure it.
E1027.body: For Atwood, the marriage is the union of Mind and Universe: “This is the union supersentient, the nuptials sublime, Mentis et Universi” [III.3 ¶15]. In the readers' summary, solitary Thought unites with the simple Understanding of its ether, and ancient mythic marriages prefigure this. Her figure for it is “the bridegroom crowneth the bride in the North” [III.3 ¶15].

E1028.summary: A verse treatise cited to illustrate that a small quantity of the composition is sealed in one glass.
E1028.body: Atwood quotes a line from Book 3 to illustrate that a small amount of the composition is sealed in one glass: “And it sufficeth in one glasse to put” [IV.3 ¶23; IV.3 n4].

E1029.summary: Planetary properties of temperament whose dominance, Atwood says, draws consciousness near the Sol principle and gives knowledge by experience.
E1029.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood speaks of “People in whom the Mars and Venus property is dominant” [APP ¶113]. She says that in such people the dominance draws consciousness near the Sol principle and gives knowledge by experience.

E1030.summary: The tincture that fixes the light of Venus in manifestation; it rises from death out of the black darkness, united with the white virginal spirit.
E1030.body: Atwood says the light of Venus cannot hold “without the masculine tincture to fix it in manifestation” [I.3 n49]. In the same note she says the tincture rises from death out of the black darkness, united with the white virginal spirit.

E1031.summary: Criticized in the Appendix: they ape the words of power but have lost the magic Key, keeping an absurd outward form.
E1031.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood criticizes the Masons. She says they ape the words of power but have lost the magic Key. Their outward form is absurd, she says, and survives only through a secret response of common sense to the original mystery [APP ¶100].

E1032.summary: The author of the Tractatus Aureus, quoted on the stone generated with Light and on dissolution by the watery Form.
E1032.body:
Atwood quotes the Master's Tractatus Aureus twice:

- **Cap. 3**, after her own gloss on Boehme, on Nature's middle principle: “Our stone comes with Light, and with Light it is generated” [III.1 ¶49; III.1 n54]. The stone is generated with Light and brings forth darkness.
- **Cap. 2**, in support of dissolution by Water, fire on the Foliated Sulphur, the King's Tincture and revival: “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!” [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n7].

E1033.summary: That whose application moves the first link in the chain of vital causes; also the concealment under which the Adepts kept the three operations.
E1033.body: Atwood writes: “The first link in the chain of vital causes moves, as we apply the Master Key.” [III.4 ¶47]. She does not explain the key there. Elsewhere she says the Adepts kept the three operations “reserved strictly under the Master Key of their Dilemma” [IV.2 ¶3], so the term also names their concealment.

E1034.summary: Only a Master mason can 'erect structures in the air'; in context this apparently means Mind working by its own reflective energy, too hard for inferior craftsmen.
E1034.body: Atwood writes: “it is the work only of a Master mason, of Grand Architects, as the Brethren have it, to erect structures in the air” [IV.2 ¶14]. She equates the Master mason with the Grand Architects of the Brethren and says the task is too onerous for inferior craftsmen. The context suggests the image stands for Mind working by its own reflective energy, but that reading is inferred, not stated.

E1035.summary: A group voice whose term “benedicta viriditas” Atwood applies to the green or purple vegetative life.
E1035.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood applies the masters' term “benedicta viriditas” to the green or purple vegetative life [APP ¶119].

E1036.summary: What the work is done on: all men have it and live by it, but few can handle it.
E1036.body: The material is what the work is done on: all men have it, but few can handle it. Atwood: “because all men have the material and live by it” [III.4 ¶2]. She does not identify the material further in this passage. See also Matter.

E1037.summary: Atwood's name for the subject whose development her Kabalistic and Greek concordances are meant to support.
E1037.body: Atwood speaks of “the development of this Material of Mind” [III.1 ¶71]. She says the Kabalistic and Greek concordances that follow will support it.

E1038.summary: For Psellus, the only means of strengthening the soul's vehicle: perfecting the soul by the power of materials on earth.
E1038.body: Atwood quotes Psellus, who calls material Rites the only means of strengthening the soul's vehicle. Their aim is “To initiate or perfect the human soul by the power of materials here on earth” [II.1 ¶51].

E1039.summary: The celestial instinct that first conceived the tree of life; it alone reveals the tree and leads into the Paternal light of life.
E1039.body: Atwood equates Maternal intelligence with the celestial instinct. She speaks of “the celestial instinct only to reveal; that subtle Maternal; intelligence which originally conceived it” [III.1 ¶34]. This intelligence first conceived the tree of life, alone reveals it, and leads into the Paternal light of life [III.1 ¶34].

E1040.summary: An unnamed voice quoted in Latin, praising the Creator's laws and foundations.
E1040.body: Atwood quotes the mathematician in Latin, illustrating praise of the Creator's laws and foundations: “En tibi Norma Poli --- ! en divae Libramina Molis!” [II.4 ¶30]. The rendering is our translation, not one the book gives.

E1041.summary: Atwood's word for the emanation's passage from flat to cubic, in the phrase 'Mathesis becoming geometric'.
E1041.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood describes the emanation passing from flat to cubic: “It is Mathesis becoming geometric.” [APP ¶66]. She gives the term no further gloss.

E1042.summary: That on which the sulphur must return for any effect to be produced.
E1042.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood says an effect requires “a return of the sulphur (this third, this obscure, this radical life) on its matrix” [APP ¶183].

E1043.summary: The Hermetic subject: one simple substance under all forms, identified with our Identity, known only in the experience and by the Fire of Intellect, not in nature.
E1043.body:
**Atwood's main account.** The Matter is diffused everywhere and partly obtainable anywhere, but the aim is to perfect it. In her words, “there is but One Matter truly qualifiable or capable of qualifying matter to be harmonized in this way” [II.1 ¶20]. It is no common water but “an unctuous mineral vapour, universally subsisting” [III.2 ¶7]. She identifies it with “the Thing itself, which is our Identity. This is the true Hermetic material” [III.2 ¶7]. In the same passage it is the power borne by Cheiron, it is Pan, and by rhetorical question it is the Water of our Sea of the old Alchemists [III.2 ¶7]. The Arabians call it Flos Salis Albi [III.2 ¶8]. Readers note that it first appears in vision in demoniacal forms [III.2 ¶7].

**The philosophers' Matter.** Atwood sets out, apparently with approval, the view of these philosophers. Matter is “the Material Principle which, according to these philosophers, the Divine experience imparts” [III.2 ¶51]. It is one and all, everywhere and nowhere, uncompounded, an Infinity, describable only by negations and apprehended by ablative reasoning and negation: “that which of itself is neither essence nor quantity, nor any one of those things, by which Being is defined” [III.2 ¶53]. It is the last and lowest effect, the inverse of the First Cause, yet “somewhat; and real” [III.2 ¶54]. She identifies it with the Quintessence of Plato, the Water of Thales, the Non-Being of Parmenides and the Abyss of the Kabalists [III.2 ¶60]. “For in the natural world there is no such Matter to be found” [III.2 ¶61]. Life and the Fire of Intellect discover “the True matter of the adepts” [III.2 ¶62].

**Matter (the One).** “The Matter of all things is One and proved simple in the experience” [III.3 ¶65]. It is Nature, “one and the same Unknown Identity through all” [III.3 ¶65], the true element chemists have never found. As non-being, it arises by severance from real being [III.3 ¶77]. When it is sacrificed in the reunion, it supplies body to the Divine.

**Other voices.** The metropolitan of Memphis says “Matter appeared: and inseparable from it attraction instantly began to operate” [III.3 ¶48]. Vaughan speaks of that without which “the Matter is not alterable as to our final purpose” [IV.2 ¶35], namely the sublimations and double nativity. A passage whose voice is unclear says the Matter must be fed leisurely, cleansed and given wings that are held back: “Cause, therefore, wings to be prepared for the Matter” [IV.1 ¶15].

**Appendix** (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860). “The Matter is seen with the inner eye” [APP ¶162], with agent and patient alternating. In handling it, it flows from the new-born consciousness through the hands to ferment another life [APP ¶164].

E1044.summary: For the prince, what is perfected and corrupted; full knowledge of this is the goal of study.
E1044.body: Atwood quotes the prince, who makes the goal of study “a plenary knowledge of the verity of perfecting and corrupting Matter and Form” [III.4 ¶20].

E1045.summary: A maxim quoted within Basil's passage, where the praise of the science lies in experience.
E1045.body: The maxim “Physician, heal thyself” appears inside a passage Atwood quotes from Basil. There, the praise of the science consists in experience [IV.1 ¶2].
